Interviewer:	Have I explained what my project is about?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	We’re looking at women engineering, although I don’t really know whether you consider your course to be an engineering or engineering-related course?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Ok we’ve taken quite a broad perspective of engineering. Is your course music technology?

Subject:	No sound technology.

Interviewer:	Sound technology. Basically we’re looking at the reasons women have decided to do engineering courses, and their experiences of higher education to try and improve the situation and the numbers of women doing engineering in the future? So I’ve just got a few questions about how your course is going and things like that. The first few questions are just some background things. Did you do A levels?

Subject:	No I did a BTEC.

Interviewer:	What was that in?

Subject:	Music technology.

Interviewer:	Was that at [university] as well?

Subject:	No that was in [town] near [city].

Interviewer:	And what type of school did you go to before that?

Subject:	I went to a girls comprehensive.

Interviewer:	Have you got any previous work experience in the industry at all?

Subject:	Yes. I started at … at 16 I went and worked in a studio in [city] for two weeks in the summer and I went and lived there. And then every year since I’ve been about 16 I do a festival called [name] down in [town] where I do stage management. Erm, also I’ve worked in (lost words). At the moment I’ve worked for the past 3 years in the students union on stage crew, doing management there as well. A bit of work with some PA companies. All my friends are in bands…

Interviewer:	That sounds like loads.

Subject:	Yeah, all my friends are in bands, so you know, if you’re the sound engineer you get dragged along to do the sound (call?)

Interviewer:	What do your parents do, are either of them in a related industry at all?

Subject:	No there’s only my Mum and she went back and did a degree a few years ago. She went back as a mature student and did archaeology and now she’s in marketing. So its completely unrelated.

Interviewer:	So why do you think that you decided to do sound technology?

Subject:	Basically when I left school I hated academic type work. I hate the fact that you know you read books and in our family, I mean we haven’t got a lot of money so you needed to go into an industry where you could earn a living and have a trade. I loved art in school, but of course you can’t make your money out of doing art really, so music was the obvious choice. And I play, but I just didn’t see a point in getting a certificate saying you can play an instrument, so I thought go into the engineering side.
Interviewer:	And was your Mum supportive of you doing that then?

Subject:	On and off. At first when I went to college I was the only girl in the class and I think that shocked her a bit. And then she saw me fiddling with electronics and things and I don’t think she saw that as the kind of thing I should be doing, but since then, when she comes and sees concerts and stuff, she’s been more supportive, when she’s witnessed what I do.

Interviewer:	Were you surprised to be the only female?

Subject:	Yes. Erm, considering I came from an all girls school as well.

Interviewer:	So it was a bit of a shock to the system?

Subject:	It was yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the type of school had any impact on your decision to do an engineering course at all? Did you have any careers advice or anything like that at school?

Subject:	No. I mean I know it sounds really sort of cliché, but in girls schools they don’t really advise engineering, which is quite bizarre so. When I said I wanted to go on and do that, I think they were quite shocked and sort of told me how difficult it was going to be and tried to put me off as much as possible from going into engineering. Erm, but as I hated school I was going to do the complete opposite to what they told me anyway, so, that’s when I decided to go and do this.

Interviewer:	Ok. How did you decide to come to [university] then?

Subject:	Erm, basically all the music technology courses that are in Britain require you to do playing and they are normally Bas or sometimes BSc’s but you do still have to play and I didn’t want to do that, I wanted to do the complete engineering side of the whole thing. So I needed sound technology and there’s only a few places in Britain that do that and [university] was one of them.

Interviewer:	When you started doing the BTEC did it concern you that there was a lack of women? Did it ever put you off?

Subject:	In a way no. In a way it made me want to do it even more. I don’t really get on with girls generally. That sounds really bizarre but I’m more of a sort of boys girl, in the way that you know, you get less bitchiness and it’s a lot more fun. People take what they do a lot more seriously a lot of the time. And so I think in a way when I came in and after getting the first few assignments back, I was one of the youngest and I was getting some of the highest grades, I think I thought ok I’m going to prove every single one of you wrong and do the best that I can, so I did.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering though?

Subject:	Yes absolutely. Generally, we’re more logical when it comes to sorting out problems anyway. So I don’t know why it’s a field that people don’t seem to look at.

Interviewer:	What do you think could be done at an earlier stage to get more women interested?

Subject:	I mean one of them is to tell them that that option’s open. When you’re at school you know it’s go and be a doctor, go and be a lawyer, go and do this, and you’re never really told about other options. You’re only told about the main options that you hear about. And engineering doesn’t happen to be one of them, so they should really tell people. Sponsorship, coming into the industry. When I first started we don’t have any money at home, so I was looking for sponsorship to do my degree, and there was none for women engineers in this area, and there still isn’t any to my knowledge. You know, there’s lots for guys but none for girls.

Interviewer:	Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer or a good sound technologist?

Subject:	Erm, logic is a big one and problem solving. Also, the ability to, you work as a team, but you do work individually a lot, so you have to be able to do both sides, as in taking orders as well as giving a lot of them and making sure that things are done when they should be done. Erm, also you’ve got to have a brain that can work scientifically in a way, but also creatively because with music you need to make it sound the way you think it should sound, but you’ve also got to know how to do that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics, like logic and problem solving would be described as either more male or female?

Subject:	I think its sort of seen that men have a more scientific brain which is complete rubbish really, because when it comes to solving problems most of the people I know on my course, don’t know how to function under that kind of pressure. Where it tends to be a characteristic in women that they stand back and quickly solve the problem as fast as it can be solved, in a logical way.

Interviewer:	Do you think then that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male dominated environment?

Subject:	Erm, I think one of the disadvantages is that people tend to double-take you. I turned up to a few sort of university interviews and I used to spell my name with an ‘e’ on the end, which is the male way, and they sort of do a double-take and say ‘you’re a girl’ and I say ‘yes I am, is that a problem’. And they’re like ‘no’, but you have to work a little bit harder I think. One of the main disadvantages is lifting equipment I find. There’s things that obviously men can do easier. They can lift heavier equipment generally. Erm, you know, I’m short, I’m only 5’3, with some of the PA stacks we bring in, they’re sort of 7 feet high, and there’s no way with my body-height ratio that I can even lift or steer that thing. So that does become an issue because guys will put their body weight behind it whereas I can’t.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages then?

Subject:	In a way yes, people tend to be quite shocked when you turn up, and it’s a very nice feeling proving everyone wrong and showing that you can actually do it better than a lot of the others can. SO that’s an advantage, and also I found that in going for job interviews, because there’s the whole equal opportunities, you do have a slight advantage in a way. If you and a guy come in with the same grades and there’s no girls in the company, they do tend to take you on because they need to be seen as doing that, and it’s a good show case for them. So I suppose that’s an opportunity in a way.

Interviewer:	I’ve got some questions about your course now. Has it been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	No. Not at all actually.

Interviewer:	Why not?

Subject:	Mainly course content I think has been a big problem. You know we’re doing sound engineering and instead of spending time doing electronics and engineering based things we’ve been told to go out and make videos, make buttons for webpages, which have absolutely nothing to do with what we’re doing, so you get the feeling its just something to pad out the course content with, which has no benefit to us whatsoever. Whereas they’re lacking in more technical details for it. 

Interviewer:	Is that what you would say has been the worst part about the course so far?

Subject:	Yes I think so. That and the amount of work really.

Interviewer:	Do you get loads of coursework and that sort of thing?

Subject:	Yes we get absolutely … I know the first year I think we got over 35-40 essays, and I mean this year we’ve got so many modules where we’ve got big group projects and when it goes down on paper, you’ve got four essays, but in our case its not because you’ve got studio time, taking the time to do it, sorting out people to get there, so you end up doing four times as much work as anybody else tends to.

Interviewer:	What would you say has been the best thing about the course then?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose the people you meet really, that tends to be the best thing wherever you are if I’m honest. I mean obviously you further your knowledge which is good and there are elements that you do love doing like getting in the studios and things, but it’s the tutors you meet are big names, and you get to talk to these people and find out sort of background knowledge and the small things that you know, you can’t learn from theory, you tend to learn from doing. I think that’s been one of the main things, and just the people you work with everyday.

Interviewer:	Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

Subject:	I’m pleased I chose the course. I think if I had to do it again, I would probably choose another university to do it in, just because the facilities here really aren’t very good. To try to get into them, you really do have to fight for your time in the studios. But also I mean there’s thing with [university] itself that just don’t function, and they haven’t been functioning. But I suppose what I’d say to that is the year I joined this course, it was the first year they ran the course, so it was a bit of a … we were the guinea pigs, and we’ve been changing things as we’ve been going along, but obviously it doesn’t change for us, it changes for the people coming after us.

Interviewer:	Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Only one in music business, none in the engineering areas at all.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Yes, I think it would be encouraging because as I said the guys that are tutoring us are very well known within the industry and if you actually had a female working there maybe the guys would get more used to realising that there is a woman in the industry that does know about this stuff, a little bit more than they do. I think that would do them all a hell of a lot of good. You know, it would be a good representation I think of girls working in this area.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor at all?

Subject:	I do. I saw him once in the first year and I’ve never seen him again.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a different personal tutor or have you just not felt the need to see your personal tutor anyway?

Subject:	I’d rather have…the guy that was actually mine, as I’ve said I met once, he’s not anything to do with our course at all, he’s in a totally unrelated school, he doesn’t know our work, doesn’t know what’s going on with us and our course, so I didn’t really see the point in them assigning him really.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	I think probably sort of my friends, if I’m honest. I mean more that pushed me through it rather than from the school, more the people I live with, that’s whats pushed me through not what the school puts behind you. From the people I’ve talked to on our course, that is the general overview of it, where you know as far as the university’s concerned, as long as they get their grades and they get the people going through everybody could break down four times a year for all they care, but as long as the work comes in that’s fine. Whereas the people that are at home actually give a damn about what’s happening not just at work but with you personally.

Interviewer:	You mentioned earlier that you have to do quite a lot of group work. When you do work in groups, do you get to choose who you work with?

Subject:	Occasionally you get to choose. The big one we’ve got this year which is 30% of our final grade, you didn’t get to choose. So you were basically put in with five other people that you didn’t know, you didn’t know what they did, and told to produce something, you know, that caused a lot of problems with a lot of people. 

Interviewer:	So it would be better if you had the opportunity to choose groups? Did you say you’re the only female on your course?

Subject:	I am yes.

Interviewer:	Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work so far then?

Subject:	Most of the group work we do.. It tends to be the people that are friends that do group work. We’ve had a few experiences where we’ve gone into the studio and I tend to know more about what I’m doing than say somebody else that’s there, and so it tends to be the fact that they don’t want to listen to what I’m saying, but more listen to what they think they should be doing and that tends to be a problem when you’re a girl, because when you’re a guy they do tend to listen to each other, and do gang up sometimes. The majority of the group work’s been ok if I’m honest.

Interviewer:	How do you cope with that then when it happens?

Subject:	Sometimes its just the typical girl thing of fine you do it your way, I’ll do it mine, then my way always comes out the way that works, then they have to sort of swallow their pride a bit. Occasionally, there have been situations where I’ve said ok I’ll sit here you do what you think you should do. They do it, it doesn’t work, then when I do it like an hour later, it functions first time and I think that sort of kicks them into place a bit.

Interviewer:	Ok, did you have the opportunity to go on a placement at all?

Subject:	There was a sort of placement year in the third year. The idea was to go away but basically you had to find your own placement, you had to fund yourself. You know the university offered no assistance in doing this. And so it just seemed a bit of a pointless exercise really. You know, I’d rather just get it all out the way. You know it was a lot of things as well, like with friends being here, I want to go through at the same time.

Interviewer:	It sounds like you’re getting a lot of experience anyway?

Subject:	Yes, but I could do with a lot more, but it tends to be where you can get your foot in the door at the times you can do it.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the best and worst things about the work experiences that you have had?

Subject:	If I’m honest I think I’ve learnt more from working in these situations than I have from sitting in a class and being told what supposedly happens. Because I mean you can be in class and then can tell you, you know, how you sort out a mixing desk say, and then you can get into a live situation and it can be a completely different story. I mean one thing I’ve learnt more from working than from class is communication with people because that’s one thing that they don’t really tend to teach you, but its one of the most important things that you need to be able to handle. Because musicians can be arsey people at the end of the day. You’ve got to try to stress to them without pissing them off what needs to be done and how it needs to be done, so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your experiences will help you when you’re trying to get a job?

Subject:	Yes, I mean in our industry it tends to be the more experience you’ve got than the amount of study you’ve got behind you. Anywhere you go you’re pretty much going to go in at bottom level but, I think work experience tends to count more than work experience does at the end of the day.

Interviewer:	Do you think you have you used what you have learnt in the work place back in the classroom?

Subject:	Yeah, I mean in studio sessions in class, because I work with different people everyday you learn how to handle these things and you learn skills like if people come in and you’re very polite to them to begin with and very professional, if something goes wrong, they’re more likely to understand about it and take a step back and let you get on with it, than if you’ve walked in, told them you’re in charge and then something goes wrong then they can be very, screaming and shouting, they get all arsey, it takes longer to do everything. I mean that’s the main thing. It’s the communication I’ve learnt that has been applied during lectures.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your course could be organised at all differently to reflect what it’s like in industry?

Subject:	Yes. I mean I think communication needs to be taught because a lot of the people that we do have on the course, the guys on the course, they can be fantastic engineers but you stick them with musicians and they piss them off within two minutes. You know, you can’t do that at the end of the day, they’re paying you’re wages. You do know what you’re doing but there has to be a fine line between telling them and negotiating with them. I mean I think that needs to be taught. There’s things like we had to set up a PA and show how you do it for one instance. And instead of actually going to a live venue and doing this for a band, you did it in a classroom, which seemed a little bit pointless because you’d never be in that situation where you had to set up a PA in an empty room for nobody to use. Its things like that that should be organised more because in theory you can sit there and rewire something in two minutes but under pressure it might take you three hours to do it and you don’t know that until you’re put into that situation.

Interviewer:	Do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you’ve finished?

Subject:	Erm, possibly a live company. I like being on the road and sort of meeting new people being in new places. I’d like to do my masters but that’s one of them things that I can’t find funding for so it’s not an option at the minute. But if I did a masters I’d probably do it in stage management so I’m sort of multi-skilled then, in the industry. But generally a touring company or a venue. I wouldn’t like to be in a studio.

Interviewer:	What do you think will be the best and the worst things about working in the industry?

Subject:	I think one of the best things will be its all new. You know you’re meeting new people you’re doing new things, I think that’s a big bonus. I mean one of the downers of it is where you’re going to be because the problem with this is you can’t just go home and find a job in your home town doing this, because you have to go where the work is. And in a way that does worry a lot of people, because you don’t know if you’re going to have to up sticks and move up to Lancashire or down south to Cornwall, it just depends whether you can find any work.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you at all?

Subject:	Erm it does in a way because I worry about if I got offered a job in September and I had to go to John O’groats for instance, I don’t have any money to go to John O’Groats, so I can’t even afford to rent a place there. So then its just completely upping sticks and going somewhere where you know nobody. In a way, you can look at it, I didn’t know anybody when I came to university and I had the best time and I met some of the best friends I’ll ever meet in my life. And in another way it can be a very lonely thing, and I think its just dependent on which way it goes.

Interviewer:	Do you think the difference when you go to university as well is that everyone is in the same boat?

Subject:	Exactly.

Interviewer:	And when you start work you are the only new person…

Subject:	And that’s just a horrible, horrible thing because people don’t know what you can do and how well you can do it. You’re just constantly under the eye for a few months. I hate that.

Interviewer:	What do you see yourself doing in say five years time?

Subject:	Erm, hopefully sort of resident in a venue somewhere. You know somewhere comfortable, just being able to do what I love doing everyday really. Erm, that’s where I’d like to be, whether that’s the case or not are two different things.

Interviewer:	What about in maybe 10 years time? Is there a good career ladder to climb in this sort of industry?

Subject:	Well, yeah. I’d love to be… I’d love to work in a studio but with world music. Erm whereas hopefully in ten years time I can choose where I want to be, with, in comparison to coming straight into the industry.

Interviewer:	So you can be more selective?

Subject:	Exactly, that’s what I’d like to do. And somewhere that pays you well.

Interviewer:	Would you like to work abroad at all?

Subject:	Yes, I’d love to go abroad and work. But I think I’d have to, for certain times in the year, you know, for a certain amount of time of the year, I would have to come home. Because, you know, I have family here, I have my friends here. I think if I just upped sticks and moved abroad, I couldn’t do that on a permanent basis. But on a semi-permanent basis, I’d really enjoy doing it.

Interviewer:	Ok. Are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I think so.

Interviewer:	Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	Only choose a different university I think.

Interviewer:	What other sort of options did you have for universities?

Subject:	I mean I think what it would be is, basically, since I’ve actually started here a lot more courses have opened up like last year.

Interviewer:	So it’s becoming more popular?

Subject:	It is becoming more popular, so maybe if I’d waited a year I’d have had a wider choice. It’s sort of oh god, you’re damned if you do and you’re damned if you don’t. But yeah, I think if I had more choice again I’d probably work for a year and then have more of a selection of where to go.

Interviewer:	I’ve nearly finished now. If you had to describe the characteristics of your industry, what five words would you use?

Subject:	Ooh that’s a really hard one. I suppose its, its fun, and its adventurous, but its very hard work. Erm and its quite a lonely industry to be in, simply for the fact that all of our tutors were in studios, they were on the road, but as soon as you want a family, you can’t do that, because you can’t be in the studio until 8o’clock in the next morning, you know, from 9 the morning before, you can’t do that. You have to function on normal times, and in our industry you don’t, you function at the times that they need you so its quite lonely with regards to that.

Interviewer:	Does that worry you in the future at all?

Subject:	No it doesn’t worry me for the simple fact that the majority of my friends are in the same industry. So we’re all going to be functioning on very bizarre timescales. Erm, my boyfriend is also in the industry, so he functions on that time.

Interviewer:	So you understand each other?

Subject:	Yeah it sort of syncs up in a way. You know, where everyone else gets up at say 8 in the morning, we don’t get up til 2 in the afternoon, but then you’ll work through until 6 the next morning and then go to bed. And you know, a lot of people don’t really get that. My mum certainly doesn’t understand, she’s a 9 to 5 woman. So with them sort of hours, she hates it.

Interviewer:	Would you describe the industry as masculine?

Subject:	Absolutely, yes. It’s very grubby work. It’s very, it’s hard lifting, you know. It’s very long hours. It’s very much a male industry.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will stay like that in the future?

Subject:	I hope not. I know that there are more women sort of going into it now.

Interviewer:	Are there more women in the years below you?

Subject:	Erm yeah. There’s sort of… On our course, they’ve been running sound tech for three years, we were the first year, but there’s still no other girls. But music tech there are more women coming into it, so its building up the same sort of momentum and stuff like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that its masculine will be problematic for you at all in the future?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t think so. I mean, I really do enjoy working in a male industry, because you know, its something different. And you can prove yourself, you’re constantly pushing yourself as well. 

Interviewer:	So you like the challenge?

Subject:	Yeah, I’m very much a sort of challenge person, where I need something to work towards and build to.

Interviewer:	Ok, that’s everything, thank you very much. Thank you for your help.

Erm, but as I hated school I was going to do the complete opposite to what they told me anyway, so, that’s when I decided to go and do this.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How did you decide to come to [university] then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, basically all the music technology courses that are in Britain require you to do playing and they are normally Bas or sometimes BSc’s but you do still have to play and I didn’t want to do that, I wanted to do the complete engineering side of the whole thing. So I needed sound technology and there’s only a few places in Britain that do that and [university] was one of them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you started doing the BTEC did it concern you that there was a lack of women? Did it ever put you off?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way no. In a way it made me want to do it even more. I don’t really get on with girls generally. That sounds really bizarre but I’m more of a sort of boys girl, in the way that you know, you get less bitchiness and it’s a lot more fun. People take what they do a lot more seriously a lot of the time. And so I think in a way when I came in and after getting the first few assignments back, I was one of the youngest and I was getting some of the highest grades, I think I thought ok I’m going to prove every single one of you wrong and do the best that I can, so I did.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes absolutely. Generally, we’re more logical when it comes to sorting out problems anyway. So I don’t know why it’s a field that people don’t seem to look at.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think could be done at an earlier stage to get more women interested?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I mean one of them is to tell them that that option’s open. When you’re at school you know it’s go and be a doctor, go and be a lawyer, go and do this, and you’re never really told about other options. You’re only told about the main options that you hear about. And engineering doesn’t happen to be one of them, so they should really tell people. Sponsorship, coming into the industry. When I first started we don’t have any money at home, so I was looking for sponsorship to do my degree, and there was none for women engineers in this area, and there still isn’t any to my knowledge. You know, there’s lots for guys but none for girls.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer or a good sound technologist?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, logic is a big one and problem solving. Also, the ability to, you work as a team, but you do work individually a lot, so you have to be able to do both sides, as in taking orders as well as giving a lot of them and making sure that things are done when they should be done. Erm, also you’ve got to have a brain that can work scientifically in a way, but also creatively because with music you need to make it sound the way you think it should sound, but you’ve also got to know how to do that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics, like logic and problem solving would be described as either more male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think its sort of seen that men have a more scientific brain which is complete rubbish really, because when it comes to solving problems most of the people I know on my course, don’t know how to function under that kind of pressure. Where it tends to be a characteristic in women that they stand back and quickly solve the problem as fast as it can be solved, in a logical way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think then that there are any particular advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in a male dominated environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think one of the disadvantages is that people tend to double-take you. I turned up to a few sort of university interviews and I used to spell my name with an ‘e’ on the end, which is the male way, and they sort of do a double-take and say ‘you’re a girl’ and I say ‘yes I am, is that a problem’. And they’re like ‘no’, but you have to work a little bit harder I think. One of the main disadvantages is lifting equipment I find. There’s things that obviously men can do easier. They can lift heavier equipment generally. Erm, you know, I’m short, I’m only 5’3, with some of the PA stacks we bring in, they’re sort of 7 feet high, and there’s no way with my body-height ratio that I can even lift or steer that thing. So that does become an issue because guys will put their body weight behind it whereas I can’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there are any advantages then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In a way yes, people tend to be quite shocked when you turn up, and it’s a very nice feeling proving everyone wrong and showing that you can actually do it better than a lot of the others can. SO that’s an advantage, and also I found that in going for job interviews, because there’s the whole equal opportunities, you do have a slight advantage in a way. If you and a guy come in with the same grades and there’s no girls in the company, they do tend to take you on because they need to be seen as doing that, and it’s a good show case for them. So I suppose that’s an opportunity in a way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve got some questions about your course now. Has it been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Not at all actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mainly course content I think has been a big problem. You know we’re doing sound engineering and instead of spending time doing electronics and engineering based things we’ve been told to go out and make videos, make buttons for webpages, which have absolutely nothing to do with what we’re doing, so you get the feeling its just something to pad out the course content with, which has no benefit to us whatsoever. Whereas they’re lacking in more technical details for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what you would say has been the worst part about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I think so. That and the amount of work really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get loads of coursework and that sort of thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes we get absolutely … I know the first year I think we got over 35-40 essays, and I mean this year we’ve got so many modules where we’ve got big group projects and when it goes down on paper, you’ve got four essays, but in our case its not because you’ve got studio time, taking the time to do it, sorting out people to get there, so you end up doing four times as much work as anybody else tends to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say has been the best thing about the course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose the people you meet really, that tends to be the best thing wherever you are if I’m honest. I mean obviously you further your knowledge which is good and there are elements that you do love doing like getting in the studios and things, but it’s the tutors you meet are big names, and you get to talk to these people and find out sort of background knowledge and the small things that you know, you can’t learn from theory, you tend to learn from doing. I think that’s been one of the main things, and just the people you work with everyday.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m pleased I chose the course. I think if I had to do it again, I would probably choose another university to do it in, just because the facilities here really aren’t very good. To try to get into them, you really do have to fight for your time in the studios. But also I mean there’s thing with [university] itself that just don’t function, and they haven’t been functioning. But I suppose what I’d say to that is the year I joined this course, it was the first year they ran the course, so it was a bit of a … we were the guinea pigs, and we’ve been changing things as we’ve been going along, but obviously it doesn’t change for us, it changes for the people coming after us.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Only one in music business, none in the engineering areas at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think it would be encouraging because as I said the guys that are tutoring us are very well known within the industry and if you actually had a female working there maybe the guys would get more used to realising that there is a woman in the industry that does know about this stuff, a little bit more than they do. I think that would do them all a hell of a lot of good. You know, it would be a good representation I think of girls working in this area.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a personal tutor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do. I saw him once in the first year and I’ve never seen him again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a different personal tutor or have you just not felt the need to see your personal tutor anyway?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d rather have…the guy that was actually mine, as I’ve said I met once, he’s not anything to do with our course at all, he’s in a totally unrelated school, he doesn’t know our work, doesn’t know what’s going on with us and our course, so I didn’t really see the point in them assigning him really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone or anything that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think probably sort of my friends, if I’m honest. I mean more that pushed me through it rather than from the school, more the people I live with, that’s whats pushed me through not what the school puts behind you. From the people I’ve talked to on our course, that is the general overview of it, where you know as far as the university’s concerned, as long as they get their grades and they get the people going through everybody could break down four times a year for all they care, but as long as the work comes in that’s fine. Whereas the people that are at home actually give a damn about what’s happening not just at work but with you personally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mentioned earlier that you have to do quite a lot of group work. When you do work in groups, do you get to choose who you work with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Occasionally you get to choose. The big one we’ve got this year which is 30% of our final grade, you didn’t get to choose. So you were basically put in with five other people that you didn’t know, you didn’t know what they did, and told to produce something, you know, that caused a lot of problems with a lot of people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it would be better if you had the opportunity to choose groups? Did you say you’re the only female on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I am yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had any particularly good or bad experiences of group work so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Most of the group work we do.. It tends to be the people that are friends that do group work. We’ve had a few experiences where we’ve gone into the studio and I tend to know more about what I’m doing than say somebody else that’s there, and so it tends to be the fact that they don’t want to listen to what I’m saying, but more listen to what they think they should be doing and that tends to be a problem when you’re a girl, because when you’re a guy they do tend to listen to each other, and do gang up sometimes. The majority of the group work’s been ok if I’m honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you cope with that then when it happens?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sometimes its just the typical girl thing of fine you do it your way, I’ll do it mine, then my way always comes out the way that works, then they have to sort of swallow their pride a bit. Occasionally, there have been situations where I’ve said ok I’ll sit here you do what you think you should do. They do it, it doesn’t work, then when I do it like an hour later, it functions first time and I think that sort of kicks them into place a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, did you have the opportunity to go on a placement at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There was a sort of placement year in the third year. The idea was to go away but basically you had to find your own placement, you had to fund yourself. You know the university offered no assistance in doing this. And so it just seemed a bit of a pointless exercise really. You know, I’d rather just get it all out the way. You know it was a lot of things as well, like with friends being here, I want to go through at the same time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It sounds like you’re getting a lot of experience anyway?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but I could do with a lot more, but it tends to be where you can get your foot in the door at the times you can do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the best and worst things about the work experiences that you have had?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If I’m honest I think I’ve learnt more from working in these situations than I have from sitting in a class and being told what supposedly happens. Because I mean you can be in class and then can tell you, you know, how you sort out a mixing desk say, and then you can get into a live situation and it can be a completely different story. I mean one thing I’ve learnt more from working than from class is communication with people because that’s one thing that they don’t really tend to teach you, but its one of the most important things that you need to be able to handle. Because musicians can be arsey people at the end of the day. You’ve got to try to stress to them without pissing them off what needs to be done and how it needs to be done, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your experiences will help you when you’re trying to get a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I mean in our industry it tends to be the more experience you’ve got than the amount of study you’ve got behind you. Anywhere you go you’re pretty much going to go in at bottom level but, I think work experience tends to count more than work experience does at the end of the day.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you have you used what you have learnt in the work place back in the classroom?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I mean in studio sessions in class, because I work with different people everyday you learn how to handle these things and you learn skills like if people come in and you’re very polite to them to begin with and very professional, if something goes wrong, they’re more likely to understand about it and take a step back and let you get on with it, than if you’ve walked in, told them you’re in charge and then something goes wrong then they can be very, screaming and shouting, they get all arsey, it takes longer to do everything. I mean that’s the main thing. It’s the communication I’ve learnt that has been applied during lectures.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your course could be organised at all differently to reflect what it’s like in industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I mean I think communication needs to be taught because a lot of the people that we do have on the course, the guys on the course, they can be fantastic engineers but you stick them with musicians and they piss them off within two minutes. You know, you can’t do that at the end of the day, they’re paying you’re wages. You do know what you’re doing but there has to be a fine line between telling them and negotiating with them. I mean I think that needs to be taught. There’s things like we had to set up a PA and show how you do it for one instance. And instead of actually going to a live venue and doing this for a band, you did it in a classroom, which seemed a little bit pointless because you’d never be in that situation where you had to set up a PA in an empty room for nobody to use. Its things like that that should be organised more because in theory you can sit there and rewire something in two minutes but under pressure it might take you three hours to do it and you don’t know that until you’re put into that situation.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what type of company you’d like to work for when you’ve finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, possibly a live company. I like being on the road and sort of meeting new people being in new places. I’d like to do my masters but that’s one of them things that I can’t find funding for so it’s not an option at the minute. But if I did a masters I’d probably do it in stage management so I’m sort of multi-skilled then, in the industry. But generally a touring company or a venue. I wouldn’t like to be in a studio.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think will be the best and the worst things about working in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think one of the best things will be its all new. You know you’re meeting new people you’re doing new things, I think that’s a big bonus. I mean one of the downers of it is where you’re going to be because the problem with this is you can’t just go home and find a job in your home town doing this, because you have to go where the work is. And in a way that does worry a lot of people, because you don’t know if you’re going to have to up sticks and move up to Lancashire or down south to Cornwall, it just depends whether you can find any work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm it does in a way because I worry about if I got offered a job in September and I had to go to John O’groats for instance, I don’t have any money to go to John O’Groats, so I can’t even afford to rent a place there. So then its just completely upping sticks and going somewhere where you know nobody. In a way, you can look at it, I didn’t know anybody when I came to university and I had the best time and I met some of the best friends I’ll ever meet in my life. And in another way it can be a very lonely thing, and I think its just dependent on which way it goes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the difference when you go to university as well is that everyone is in the same boat?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And when you start work you are the only new person…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And that’s just a horrible, horrible thing because people don’t know what you can do and how well you can do it. You’re just constantly under the eye for a few months. I hate that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you see yourself doing in say five years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, hopefully sort of resident in a venue somewhere. You know somewhere comfortable, just being able to do what I love doing everyday really. Erm, that’s where I’d like to be, whether that’s the case or not are two different things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about in maybe 10 years time? Is there a good career ladder to climb in this sort of industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well, yeah. I’d love to be… I’d love to work in a studio but with world music. Erm whereas hopefully in ten years time I can choose where I want to be, with, in comparison to coming straight into the industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you can be more selective?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly, that’s what I’d like to do. And somewhere that pays you well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you like to work abroad at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I’d love to go abroad and work. But I think I’d have to, for certain times in the year, you know, for a certain amount of time of the year, I would have to come home. Because, you know, I have family here, I have my friends here. I think if I just upped sticks and moved abroad, I couldn’t do that on a permanent basis. But on a semi-permanent basis, I’d really enjoy doing it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Only choose a different university I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What other sort of options did you have for universities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I mean I think what it would be is, basically, since I’ve actually started here a lot more courses have opened up like last year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s becoming more popular?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is becoming more popular, so maybe if I’d waited a year I’d have had a wider choice. It’s sort of oh god, you’re damned if you do and you’re damned if you don’t. But yeah, I think if I had more choice again I’d probably work for a year and then have more of a selection of where to go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ve nearly finished now. If you had to describe the characteristics of your industry, what five words would you use?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh that’s a really hard one. I suppose its, its fun, and its adventurous, but its very hard work. Erm and its quite a lonely industry to be in, simply for the fact that all of our tutors were in studios, they were on the road, but as soon as you want a family, you can’t do that, because you can’t be in the studio until 8o’clock in the next morning, you know, from 9 the morning before, you can’t do that. You have to function on normal times, and in our industry you don’t, you function at the times that they need you so its quite lonely with regards to that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that worry you in the future at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No it doesn’t worry me for the simple fact that the majority of my friends are in the same industry. So we’re all going to be functioning on very bizarre timescales. Erm, my boyfriend is also in the industry, so he functions on that time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you understand each other?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah it sort of syncs up in a way. You know, where everyone else gets up at say 8 in the morning, we don’t get up til 2 in the afternoon, but then you’ll work through until 6 the next morning and then go to bed. And you know, a lot of people don’t really get that. My mum certainly doesn’t understand, she’s a 9 to 5 woman. So with them sort of hours, she hates it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you describe the industry as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Absolutely, yes. It’s very grubby work. It’s very, it’s hard lifting, you know. It’s very long hours. It’s very much a male industry.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will stay like that in the future?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope not. I know that there are more women sort of going into it now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there more women in the years below you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm yeah. There’s sort of… On our course, they’ve been running sound tech for three years, we were the first year, but there’s still no other girls. But music tech there are more women coming into it, so its building up the same sort of momentum and stuff like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that its masculine will be problematic for you at all in the future?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t think so. I mean, I really do enjoy working in a male industry, because you know, its something different. And you can prove yourself, you’re constantly pushing yourself as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you like the challenge?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m very much a sort of challenge person, where I need something to work towards and build to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that’s everything, thank you very much. Thank you for your help.
